planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in autumn 4-6 inches deep in cool, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but sharply drained acidic soil in dappled woodland shade.

directions: Grow this Sino-Himalayan bulb in a cool, sheltered woodland border where summers stay mild and soil never dries out or becomes waterlogged; a raised bed of leaf mold and grit over clay works well. In early-to-midsummer, wiry stems carry nodding, outward-facing bowls of white to soft pink, each petal blotched with maroon-purple spots reminiscent of a small martagon lily. Plants are slow from seed, often taking four to six years to flower, so most gardeners start with dormant bulbs and top-dress annually with leaf mold rather than manure. Mulch for winter protection in zone 6 gardens and shield from late spring frosts, which can damage emerging shoots.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in a sheltered, frost-free shade bed with moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil.

directions: Native to the mountain forests of Taiwan, this close relative of the more common Japanese fatsia carries bolder, more deeply cut and finely toothed leaflets on a rounded evergreen frame, giving a lacier tropical texture to shaded courtyards and understory plantings. Sprays of small cream flower balls appear in autumn, followed by clusters of black berries that persist into winter and draw birds. It performs best tucked against a warm wall or beneath high tree canopy where it is shielded from hard frost, wind, and scorching midday sun, since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than Fatsia japonica. Cut back leggy stems hard in spring to keep the plant dense and encourage fresh, glossy new growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in a sheltered woodland site with moist, acidic, humus-rich soil away from harsh winter wind.

directions: This Japanese Ericaceae relative of redvein enkianthus produces slender, arching racemes of deep wine-red, fringed bells that dangle beneath the branches from mid-spring into early summer, a richer and darker color than most enkianthus. Fresh green summer foliage turns a vivid ruby red in autumn, giving strong two-season interest in a shaded shrub border alongside rhododendrons and azaleas. It is less cold-hardy and slower growing than Enkianthus campanulatus, so site it in a protected spot out of drying winter wind and mulch the root zone to buffer soil temperature swings. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and avoid letting the shallow root system dry out during summer heat.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
